 | D52 | A worked delegate/externals example, actually executed — and the eager-lookup bug it caught | **`examples/calc-delegate.gram.md`: a small `calc-js`-derived calculator (`Expr`/`Term`/`Power`/`Factor`) where `+ - * /` keep ordinary inline `{% %}` actions, `^` (`Power`) delegates to an embedded, argument-free `### Pow` implementation, `round(…)` delegates to a parameterized `Round(2)` WITH an embedded `### Round` implementation (the literal `2` threading through as a real second parameter), and a bare function call (`IDENT '(' Expr ')'`) delegates to `Call` with deliberately NO embedded implementation, left for a consuming host to supply via `setExternals`. Verified genuinely end to end, not just golden-text-diffed: `BackendJsExternalsExecSuite` (JVM-only, `core/.jvm/src/test/scala/gramaire`) lexes+parses a real input string through the example's own `## Tokens`/rules into a real `Cst` (`ConformanceLexers.tokensLexerOf` + `Table.buildTablesForP` + `Parser.run`, over the SAME undesugared `Grammar` `IR.buildIRP` builds from — `IR.irGrammarOf`'s own "flattened in `Table.productions` order" comment is why one production numbering serves both), feeds the serialized `Cst.toJson` into `BackendJs.emit`'s actual output, and RUNS it in a real, standalone ECMAScript engine (`org.openjdk.nashorn:nashorn-core`, a new `core` `.jvmSettings`-only `Test` dependency — JVM-portable, no external `node`/browser needed, so it runs under plain `sbt test` including CI's `core` job, which has no Node on `PATH`). Doing this surfaced a real bug D51 shipped undetected (its own test suite, `BackendJsSuite`, only ever golden-diffed emitted text, never ran it): a bare `-> name` delegate with NO embedded implementation rendered as a literal `externals["name"]` array element — a property READ evaluated once, eagerly, at `const actions = [...]` construction time, before a host's own `setExternals(...)` call (itself exported FROM the same module) could possibly have run yet, permanently freezing `undefined` into that `actions[]` slot; `setExternals` reassigns the `externals` *binding*, which can never retroactively fix an already-read array element. Fixed by wrapping that one case in the same lazy closure shape the parameterized path already used for an unrelated reason (`(c) => (externals[name])(c)`), deferring the lookup to every real `evaluate(cst)` call — by which point `setExternals` has had its chance. `BackendJsSuite`'s matching assertion updated to check for the wrapped form (and to assert the bare, unwrapped form is now ABSENT).** | The stated point of this phase was a worked example that actually demonstrates the feature, not just parses — so it was built to the same bar this project already holds other backends to (`check-atn-ts-parity.mjs` compiles+runs emitted TypeScript; `check-scala-peg-parity.mjs` compiles+runs emitted Scala), just scoped to a single JVM-test-only dependency (`nashorn-core`) instead of a second CI job, since `BackendJs`'s output is plain, dependency-free ECMAScript with nothing else to stand up. The bug this caught is exactly the risk golden-text assertions can't see: `BackendJsSuite`'s own tests for the D51 phase all passed while shipping output that would `TypeError` on every single real invocation of an unresolved bare delegate — string-shape correctness and runtime correctness are different claims, and only the second is what a grammar author or a consuming host actually experiences. |
 | D53 | `lint`'s `caselessLoss`: a silently WRONG export, not just a silently lossy one | **`GramaireLint.caselessLoss` (`--target antlr` only) catches a qualitatively different failure mode than D50's original three checks or this same phase's own `altLabelLoss`/`predicateLoss`: those all silently DROP a decoration or a guard, but the exported `.g4` still accepts (a superset of) the same strings on the symbols it does render. A `@caseless` token class (`IRTokenClass.caseless`, D35) is different — confirmed empirically that `BackendAntlr.scala`'s `lexerRule` renders `cls.pattern` through `regexToAntlr` completely UNCHANGED, with no case-folding and no ANTLR4 `caseInsensitive` option emitted, so the generated lexer rule matches only the EXACT case spelled in the source pattern. The exported grammar therefore accepts a strictly NARROWER language than the one actually declared — e.g. a caseless `SELECT` keyword stops matching `select`/`Select` post-export — silently WRONG output a grammar author could ship and only discover when real lowercase input a caseless class was supposed to admit gets rejected, not merely a diagnostic-quality regression. `BackendBison.scala` was checked too and found genuinely N/A: Bison emits no lexer patterns at all (`%token` names only — lexis is Flex's job, a separate `.l` file this exporter never produces), so there is no rendered pattern for `caseless` to corrupt there; the check is deliberately `antlr`-only, not asymmetric by omission.** | Broken out as its own decision, per this phase's own stated rule (lean toward growing D50's row in place for "more checks in the same command," a new row only for a genuinely new *class* of finding): "accepts a different language than intended" is a strictly more dangerous failure than "loses a decoration downstream tooling wanted," since it can pass every naive glance at the emitted `.g4` (the rule text looks entirely plausible) and only fails on real input at the exact case the source grammar meant to admit — worth flagging as its own decision rather than folding silently into the same bucket as `precedenceLoss`/`delegateLoss`/`externalsLoss`/`altLabelLoss`/`predicateLoss`, all five of which are "vanishes, doesn't corrupt." |
 | D54 | ANTLR4 predicate round-trip: export rendering; ANTLR3 gated predicates stay out of scope | **`BackendAntlr.altText` now reads `IRRule.predicate`, closing the export half of D50's own `predicateLoss` finding: a predicate rule renders back as ANTLR4's native `{ ... }?` syntax, leading the alt (idiomatic ANTLR4 style; position doesn't affect re-import, since `ConvertAntlr.atomFrom`'s `TPred` case parses a predicate at any position and `promotablePredicate` re-promotes it to trailing `{%? %}` regardless). The body is read via `r.actions.values.headOption`, never a hardcoded key name — confirmed empirically that `IR.irGrammarOf` stores it under `"default"`, but the real `emit` pipeline (`Main.scala`) always calls `IR.withActionLang` before any backend runs, re-tagging that key to the document's declared `%lang` first; a hardcoded `"default"` lookup would have silently rendered an empty `{}?` for every real grammar with a declared language. `GramaireLint.predicateLoss` now exempts `antlr` alongside `ir` (mirroring D51's `js` exemption for `delegateLoss`/`externalsLoss` once a backend actually renders what it used to drop) — `bison` stays flagged, since yacc has no predicate concept to render into. Two of `ConvertAntlr`'s existing import-side drops were investigated for fixability and found structurally unfixable at the current grammar-model level, not merely unconverted: a predicate sharing an alt with an action (`Alt.action: Option[String]` is one slot serving both purposes, per D42's own lexical `isPredicate` check on that same field) and a predicate nested inside a group (`Sym.Group`'s inner alternatives are bare `Vector[Sym]`, no action slot at all) — both keep their existing drop-and-warn behavior, now with warning text naming the specific structural reason instead of a generic "no Core equivalent." **ANTLR3-style gated predicates (`{pred}? => alt`) are explicitly out of scope** — Gramaire's ANTLR converter targets ANTLR4 only; a `.g4` using that syntax continues to fail import exactly as before (`lexG4`'s "unexpected character `>`"), deliberately not patched over.** | Predicates that survived import were previously lost silently on export — a grammar author converting ANTLR4 → Gramaire → ANTLR4 got a *different*, unconditionally-wider accepted language back, exactly the failure `predicateLoss` exists to catch, just previously uncaught for the one backend (`antlr`) that could actually fix it rather than merely flag it. Scoped to ANTLR4 only per an explicit team decision, not an oversight: ANTLR4 itself removed the older syntactic-predicate construct (`(alt)=>`, ANTLR2/3) once ALL(\*) could resolve that class of ambiguity via full-context prediction instead of hand-written backtracking lookahead, so a real ANTLR4 `.g4` file never contains ANTLR3 gated-predicate syntax for this converter to need to read in the first place — building support for it would mean targeting a dead dialect, not the format ANTLR authors actually write today. The two import-side drop cases were confirmed empirically against the actual `Alt`/`Sym.Group` shapes (not assumed) before being scoped out, matching this document's own "verified against the real source, not the notation's docs in the abstract" convention (D50/D53). |
+| D55 | Simplified-view idiom recognition (`DiagramNormalize`) always bails out on an action-bearing alternative | **`Railroad.diagramOf`'s `Simplified` branch now calls `DiagramNormalize.simplify`, which pattern-matches a rule's `Diagram.Stack` for two shapes — an alternative that's a strict prefix of another (rewritten to that prefix plus an `Optional` tail) and a stack of direct-left-recursive alternatives plus one base alternative (rewritten to `base` followed by a `ZeroOrMore` of the recursive tail(s)) — closing the "first shipped step" the railroad-renderer-roadmap's phase 4 already named as the target. `simplify` checks `hasAction(alts)` first and returns the diagram unchanged if any alt carries a `{% %}`/`{%? %}` `ActionCaption`: an action's evaluation order and binding belong to one specific alternative, and collapsing that alternative into a shared `Optional`/`ZeroOrMore` tail would silently relocate or drop it — a real bug caught before this landed (the drafted module, found already on disk uncommitted, had no such guard). Wider idioms — separated lists (`X (',' X)*`), general factorization, 3+-alternative stacks with no single recognized shape — are explicitly out of scope until they have the same kind of test-backed equivalence coverage; `source` stays byte-stable regardless of any of this, since only the `Simplified` branch calls `simplify` at all.** | Landing the "first shipped step" of an already-committed-to phase, not a new scope decision — the roadmap had named idiom recognition as the next milestone once the diagram AST and view plumbing existed; this is that step, scoped to exactly the two shapes with a real test (an obvious optional tail, a direct-left-recursive chain) rather than a broader factorization pass no equivalence-test suite yet backs (docs/railroad-renderer-roadmap.md's own "Non-goals" section records the broader restraint). |
+| D56 | `.gram.lock` records which `--diagram-view` produced committed artifacts, for provenance only | **A `diagramView` field on the sidecar `Lock`, following the exact optional/omit-when-default convention `sourceLayout` already established (D-numbered implicitly by that field's own prior addition): absent — and never written when `Source` — so every lock predating this field, and every lock `fmt` writes under the still-default `Source` view, keeps round-tripping byte-for-byte; present as `"diagramView": "simplified"` only when `--diagram-view=simplified` produced the committed sidecar SVGs. Like `sourceLayout`, `checkStructure`/`checkDrift` don't key on it at all — both classify a document from its fence content and headings alone, never from which view rendered a committed diagram, so this is maintainer-facing provenance, not a new gate.** | Closes a real, previously-silent gap: nothing on disk recorded which view produced a grammar's committed diagrams, so a maintainer (or a future audit) had no way to tell "simplified" from "source" short of re-running `fmt` and diffing. Deliberately not wired into `checkDrift` — the lock already has one established convention for a provenance-only field (`sourceLayout`), and this reuses it rather than inventing a second one. |
+| D57 | Railroad node navigation is shared code (`site/src/lab/railroadNav.ts`), bound to the renderer's own `data-rr-*` grouping | **Both the Lab and the Notebook island now bind nonterminal-node hover/click/keyboard navigation through one shared `bindRailroadNodeNav` helper, querying the `<g class="rr-node rr-node-nonterm" data-rr-kind="..." data-rr-label="...">` grouping `Railroad.scala`'s `renderSvg` already emits (railroad-renderer-roadmap's phase 3, "semantic affordances" — this is the "built from that structure" half that hadn't landed yet). The Lab's own hover/click cross-highlight (pre-existing) was migrated off querying `rect.rr-nonterm` plus its text sibling separately (two listener targets per node, because the text painted on top of the rect) onto one listener on the `<g>` itself. The Notebook, which had no diagram interactivity at all, gets the same click/keyboard "jump to that rule's cell" affordance the outline sidebar already had (`jumpToRule`, resolving a label to a block index the same way `jumpToOutlineEntry` does). Every click/keydown handler calls `stopPropagation()`, since both islands nest the diagram inside a larger click/keydown-handling container (a cell's own "click to edit" surface, in the Notebook's case) — activating a nonterminal reference must navigate, never also trigger the ancestor's own activation.** | The metadata already existed (per-node `<title>`/`data-rr-*`, shipped earlier) but nothing consumed it — the Lab's interactivity predated that metadata and was never migrated, and the Notebook never got equivalent interactivity built at all. One shared module rather than two islands growing their own subtly-diverging DOM-query logic; verified end-to-end against the real Scala.js engine (not mocked), including that navigating never also opens the source cell it navigated from. |

 Every new phase must preserve deterministic output, stay test-backed, and keep
 the source-vs-simplified distinction explicit in the artifact itself.
+
+## Non-goals
+
+- No runtime dependency on an external railroad-diagram generator (RR,
+  Tab Atkins' `railroad-diagrams`, DrawGrammar, ebnsf, or similar) — they're
+  design references for vocabulary and layout ideas, never a linked library
+  or a `fmt`-time subprocess. `Railroad.scala` stays the one renderer, in
+  Scala, cross-built to the JVM CLI and the site's Scala.js engine alike.
+- No default grammar-shaping rewrite. RR's factorization and
+  direct-recursion elimination are real, useful transformations, but they
+  change what a diagram visually claims about the grammar's shape — anything
+  in that family only ever ships as an explicit, named, test-backed
+  normalization pass behind a non-default view (`DiagramNormalize`, phase 4
+  above), never folded into `source` or turned on by default.
